title: Buffalo Bills 2026 watch guide: TV, streaming info for Josh Allen and Super Bowl hopefuls We break down how Bills Mafia can watch every game this season and how much it all costs, for both in- and out-of-market fans. Steven Louis Goldstein 2

full_text:
Will this be the year that Josh Allen and Buffalo finally break through? Nic Antaya / Getty Images
It’s a new season with a new stadium, but the singularity of Buffalo Bills culture remains the same.
Buffalo is where fans leap through tables and volunteer to shovel snow off of turf. The Bills are still fueled by Josh Allen’s arm, James Cook’s legs, Dion Dawkins’ strength and Damar Hamlin’s spirit. As always, the question lingers … is this the year?
First-year head coach Joe Brady helms an impressive roster. Allen is a perennial MVP candidate, while Cook is the NFL’s reigning rushing king. The front office has made some inspired all-in moves, adding DJ Moore out wide and Bradley Chubb off the edge. Buffalo has reached either the divisional round or the AFC Championship Game in the last six postseasons. There’s a clear Super Bowl mandate for 2026.
The team is lined up for six primetime games — including a blockbuster on Thanksgiving versus the Kansas City Chiefs — and another spotlight on Christmas afternoon against the Denver Broncos. Accordingly, we’ve put together this guide to the necessary channels and streamers. Follow the Bills on The Athletic feed; tap in with beat reporter (and Buffalo State grad!) Joe Buscaglia .
All times listed below are ET.
The most expansive option for live game coverage is a multichannel plan. That includes streamers like Fubo, Sling TV and YouTube TV, or more traditional providers like DirecTV, Dish and Xfinity. We lay out cord-cutting alternatives for each NFL media partner down below, but there’s a certain peace of mind to the consolidation of pay television.
Main window: Sunday afternoon (in-market fans)
Playoffs: 1 wild-card game, 1 divisional game, AFC Championship Game
Each week, CBS carries games across two Sunday kickoff slots: one at 1 p.m., and another at 4:05 p.m. or the national window at 4:25 p.m. There will be 10 nationwide Sunday doubleheaders this year on CBS. Broadcasts are set by region when there are multiple offerings in a spot.
The Bills are also slated to play in a special Saturday showdown airing on CBS in Week 15. They host the Chicago Bears on the night of Dec. 19.
It’s not a clean split, but CBS is known as the primary home of the AFC. The network’s theme music is a certified slapper.
Its main pregame show, “The NFL Today,” adds recent retirees Russell Wilson and Kyle Long to its studio crew. CBS announcers include Jim Nantz and Ian Eagle, while the color commentary rotation stars JJ Watt.
What you’ll need to watch: A pay TV package, or an indoor TV antenna for free over-the-air viewing. Local CBS games also stream on Paramount+.
Main window: Sunday afternoon (in-market fans)
Playoffs: 1 wild-card game, 1 divisional game, NFC Championship Game
Like CBS, Fox splits Sunday afternoons between early 1 p.m. action and later 4:05/4:25 p.m. matchups. Its centerpiece is branded as “America’s Game of the Week.” Unlike CBS, Fox has a dancing robot named Cleatus . It’s the nominal network for the NFC as well.
Kevin Burkhardt, Joe Davis and Adam Amin are the lead play-by-play voices. Burkhardt pairs with Tom Brady, while Davis calls games alongside Greg Olsen. Amin is partnered with newcomer Drew Brees, who is fresh off his Pro Football Hall of Fame induction. Some Spanish-language broadcasts are available on Fox Deportes.
What you’ll need to watch: A pay TV package, or an antenna for free over-the-air viewing. Local Fox games also stream on Fox One.
Main window: Sunday afternoon (out-of-market fans)
These two are the access points for all non-national matchups that aren’t on regional CBS or Fox.
NFL Sunday Ticket has full games. It’s exclusive to YouTube and YouTube TV. Those without a YouTube TV plan can still get NFL Sunday Ticket as a primetime channel through the standard YouTube app.
RedZone is the whip-around program that jumps around the slate to cover scoring drives. This is the place for Scott Hanson , “the witching hour” and chaotic octobox split screens. It can be added to NFL Sunday Ticket, and it’s included on some high-end pay TV sports plans.
RedZone also lives on NFL+ Premium, which can be bundled with the ESPN Unlimited plan.
What you’ll need to watch: An NFL Sunday Ticket subscription through YouTube TV or the YouTube app; NFL RedZone access through select pay TV packages, ESPN Unlimited or NFL+ Premium.
Playoffs: 2 wild-card games, 1 divisional game
This is the faithful home of “Sunday Night Football” each weekend. And because everything has to be confusing, the NBC lineup opens with a Wednesday night season premiere. The Bills’ Thanksgiving clash with the Chiefs is also under the “Sunday Night Football” brand … on a Thursday night. At least SNF has a consistent 8:20 p.m. start time.
Mike Tirico and Cris Collinsworth are in the booth, with Melissa Stark reporting from the sidelines. Carrie Underwood sings about waiting all day for Sunday night . NBC’s “Football Night in America” pregame show brings on longtime head coach Mike Tomlin. Telemundo has the telecasts in Spanish.
The network has two extra Saturday offerings for Week 17. One is exclusive to Peacock, and both matchups will be announced later in the season. The same goes for NBC’s Week 18 regular-season finale.
“Sunday Night Football” is subject to flex scheduling — games can be swapped in and out of the window twice between Weeks 5-10 and any time from Weeks 11-17. This allows executives to pick games with greater playoff implications, though it leaves the actual ticket holders in a bind.
What you’ll need to watch: A pay TV package, or an antenna for free over-the-air viewing, or a Peacock account with the live sports plan.
Playoffs: 1 wild-card game, 1 divisional game, Super Bowl LXI
The Disney networks combine to cover 17 “Monday Night Football” games. Ten of those are on both ABC and ESPN, with another seven exclusive to the latter. The oft-maligned “Monday Night Football” doubleheader is now a thing of the past.
MNF kickoffs have 8:15 p.m. starts, and their schedule flexes can happen any time in Weeks 12-17. The two Saturday ABC/ESPN matchups in Week 18 will be set as the postseason picture sharpens.
ESPN is preparing for its first Super Bowl broadcast ever on Feb. 14, 2027. It will be simulcast on ABC.
Joe Buck handles play-by-play for MNF. He’s joined by analyst Troy Aikman, plus the sideline duo of Lisa Salters and Laura Rutledge. Spanish-language airings can be found on ESPN Deportes. For 12 regular-season games and the Super Bowl, ESPN2 offers an alternate “ManningCast,” in which Eli and Peyton Manning watch the games with famous fans. Guests have ranged from Bill Belichick to Lil Wayne .
What you’ll need to watch: A pay TV package, or an antenna for ABC, or an ESPN Unlimited account.
Main window: Thursday night
Playoffs: 1 wild-card game
Most weeks begin with “Thursday Night Football,” which kicks off at 8:15 p.m. Those games are behind the Prime paywall, but they’re free over the air in the participants’ home markets. Flex rules around TNF are a bit less hectic, with two allotments between Weeks 13-17.
Thursdays are called by Al Michaels and Kirk Herbstreit, with Kaylee Hartung on sideline duty. Herbstreit loves dogs ; Michaels hates vegetables . Prime has Spanish-language coverage and advanced stat broadcast options within its app. Former Bills quarterback Ryan Fitzpatrick is one of the pregame, halftime and postgame personalities. His shirtless antics in Buffalo are not weather-contingent.
What you’ll need to watch: Amazon Prime. TNF is also free on Twitch with a registered account.
The league-owned media outlet is now under ESPN’s purview, thanks to a blockbuster deal that gave the NFL a 10 percent ownership stake in “The Worldwide Leader in Sports.” As of July 30, NFL Network is integrated into the ESPN Unlimited plan. It can also be accessed through NFL+ or NFL+ Premium.
NFL Network has five of the international games, plus a pair of Saturday matchups in Week 16 to be revealed at least two weeks prior to Dec.…

full_text:
Quarterback Caleb Williams and most of the Bears offense are back from their NFC North championship season. It's a different story on defense. Nic Antaya / Getty Images
The Chicago Bears didn’t claim any players off waivers. That is not the best barometer for how a team will perform in the upcoming season, but it tells us how general manager Ryan Poles and coach Ben Johnson feel about the locker room.
Sometimes, a team can strike gold with waiver claims, as the Bears did with cornerback Josh Blackwell in 2022 or linebacker D’Marco Jackson last year. Often, those waiver claims don’t have much impact.
When the Bears report to Halas Hall on Tuesday, they’ll likely have close to the 53-man roster they’ll bring to Carolina for Week 1, along with a practice squad. The defending division champs continued to distance themselves from the Matt Eberflus era by trading Gervon Dexter and waiving 2023 fifth-round pick Terell Smith and 2024 third-round pick Kiran Amegadjie.
What stands out about the 2026 post-cuts roster? Here’s our annual by-the-numbers breakdown:
The experience in the Bears’ quarterbacks room continues to be a strength. Caleb Williams has started all 34 games. His backup Tyson Bagent has four career starts, and Case Keenum has 66. We saw that play out in the preseason when Bagent and Keenum had strong performances, helping lift some of the younger players. And Williams now has two seasons’ worth of NFL games, plus two postseason games, to lean on.
For context, this number would have been four in 2024 ahead of Williams’ rookie season. At the start of 2023, Justin Fields’ third season, the total starts for the quarterbacks room was 29. In 2019, Mitch Trubisky’s third season, the room had 30 combined starts.
How rare is it for the Bears to open with the same three QBs on their active roster in consecutive seasons? The last time it happened in back-to-back years was 2014-15 (Jay Cutler, Jimmy Clausen and David Fales).
As Williams continues to ascend and cement himself as a long-term starting quarterback, that number will matter less and less. For Year 3 — and Year 2 with Johnson — it’s a positive.
The offense put up 6,447 yards last season and lost only 1,183 of those in the offseason, with wide receiver DJ Moore getting traded to Buffalo and wide receiver Olamide Zaccheaus moving to Atlanta in free agency. The 53-man roster includes more than 80 percent of that yardage with running backs D’Andre Swift and Kyle Monangai, wide receivers Rome Odunze and Luther Burden, and tight ends Colston Loveland and Cole Kmet. That’s rare continuity for this franchise.
Last season, the Bears ranked second in the NFL in offensive yards coming from players 25 or younger, and all those players are back.
This number stays steady with the return of tight end Cole Kmet, cornerback Jaylon Johnson and kicker Cairo Santos. That August 2020 decision to bring in Santos proved to be one that has had a lasting impact on the franchise. He’s in the third year of the four-year contract extension he signed at the end of the 2023 season. Kmet and Johnson were the first picks for Pace of the 2020 draft, as each one enters Year 7 as the longest-tenured Bears.
“He’s an unbelievable player, unbelievable corner,” Kmet said of Johnson during training camp. “It’s been awesome to be with him since we’ve been drafted. I do joke that I still am the longest-tenured Bear by like 15 minutes. But yeah, that being said, Jaylon and I have been through a lot together, and no one’s rooting for him more than I am this year. That’s for sure. “
This is one more than last year , which was Ben Johnson’s first season at the helm. More salary-cap constraints mixed with contract flexibility put the Bears in position to add 21 new players, which is also a sign of Johnson and defensive coordinator Dennis Allen continuing to put their stamp on the team. The 11 rookies also add to that number.
The Bears will likely have as many undrafted rookies on their Week 1 roster as they did in 2023-25 combined. This is the most UDFAs they’ve carried entering the start of the season since 2022, when they had six undrafted rookies in Poles’ first year. Only one of those players, cornerback Josh Blackwell, remains a Bear, though they could still re-sign linebacker Jack Sanborn.
They carried four on their initial 53-man roster but are expected to place tight end Hayden Large on injured reserve. Large provides an H-back option and someone who can be effective on special teams when he’s healthy. Safety Skyler Thomas, defensive tackle Jayden Loving and long snapper Beau Gardner all earned roster spots this summer.
The Bears traded Dexter to Atlanta, leaving them without their leading sack getter from the interior over the past two seasons. He had six sacks last season, but the fit with Allen’s scheme clearly wasn’t where they hoped it would be entering Dexter’s contract year. Jordan van den Berg’s ascent helped, but he’s a rookie. Grady Jarrett had only 1.5 sacks last season as he battled through a knee injury. Newcomer Neville Gallimore had 3.5 and Kentavius Street had one.
Jimmy Kempski of the Philly Voice compiles this every season, and the Bears’ roster as of Sunday evening was its oldest since 2021, when they had the oldest roster in the league entering Pace and Matt Nagy’s final season.
The number does require some explanation, as Keenum is 38 but likely won’t play all season. Next is Santos, 34, at a position where age is just a number. Then there’s Joe Thuney, 33, who showed no sign of aging last year when he was named the league’s top offensive lineman. That makes the overall age more palatable, combined with the core of talent 27 and younger, which includes 14 starters.
This wasn’t surprising based on how the offseason went, but it was still startling to see. Only defensive ends Austin Booker, Montez Sweat, linebacker D’Marco Jackson and Jaylon Johnson remain from the starting lineup in the loss to the Rams.
Linebacker T.J. Edwards couldn’t play because of his ankle injury. Nickelback Kyler Gordon, who’s on the PUP list, came off the bench, as did cornerback Tyrique Stevenson.
In 2019, the Bears’ roster had all but two starters from both sides of the ball in that team’s playoff loss the previous season.
The overhaul of the defense means new starters at defensive tackle, linebacker and both safety spots. Despite leading the league in takeaways, the Bears weren’t going to keep the same group that allowed too many yards last season. That’s a good thing, but overhauled doesn’t mean better. It’s faster and younger, but injuries are a concern. This kind of turnover isn’t necessarily a bad thing, just somewhat eye-opening for a reigning division winner.

Caleb Williams enters Year 3 for the Chicago Bears as reigning NFC North champions. Patrick McDermott / Getty Images
Last season, the Chicago Bears smashed their 7.5-win total with an 11-6 run to their first NFC North title since 2018. To start this season, they’re sitting third on the list of odds to win the division.
Their +305 odds give them a 23 percent implied probability to defend their crown, so they’re not far behind the Detroit Lions at +175 (33 percent) — or the Green Bay Packers at +240 (27 percent).
My model forecasts a similarly close race that actually positions the Bears slightly ahead of the Packers. Let’s run through his model’s projections and dive into how close it could really be between the Bears and Lions.
The Bears are a tricky team to project heading into the season.
First and foremost, they won seven one-score games last year, which leads me to believe that will regress a little bit. The defense also leaves something to be desired after finishing last season 30th in Expected Points Added (EPA) per play when excluding turnovers. And while I believe coach Ben Johnson is one of the best offensive minds in football, and that being paired with Caleb Williams for another season should take the offense to a new level, how Williams’ development in Year 3 will be the key to their season.
The clearest reason the Bears aren’t favored to win the division, though, is because of their schedule. They play the toughest schedule in the NFC North by a decent margin, the 19th-toughest in the league. An average team would be expected to win 8.5 of those games. By comparison, the Lions play the third-easiest schedule, which an average team would be expected to win nine of those games.
The Lions also grade out as the better team in my model. The Bears have the higher upside on offense, but the Lions have the safer floor. Jared Goff, Jahmyr Gibbs and Amon-Ra St. Brown coupled with a re-tooled offensive line is a good place to start. The defense does give me some pause — especially with defensive backs Brian Branch and Kerby Joseph not able to suit up for at least the first month of the season — but their front seven led by Aidan Hutchinson and Jack Campbell gives the Lions the edge there, too.
Still, these teams aren’t separated by much. In fact, on a neutral field, my model would favor the Lions by less than a half-point. It’s close, but every factor has to be taken into account when running season simulations, and the question of how Williams develops coupled with the Lions’ favorable schedule is enough to give Detroit the lead in my projections.

full_text:
Dillon Gabriel completed 12 of 15 passes for 186 yards and three touchdowns in the Browns’ preseason finale, which perhaps made releasing him more difficult. Ken Blaze / Imagn Images via Reuters Connect
Dillon Gabriel has finally found his place in the Browns’ quarterback room.
It’s almost perfect. The Browns can keep him without committing to him. Gabriel remains under contract and eligible to return, but he doesn’t occupy one of the 53 active roster spots. Cleveland begins the season with Deshaun Watson, Shedeur Sanders and Taylen Green, while delaying another decision on the quarterback who has spent his entire career in organizational limbo.
Good enough to keep. Rarely good enough to choose.
The timing of Gabriel’s back injury certainly is convenient. Gabriel entered Thursday’s preseason finale against New England seemingly competing with Green for the third quarterback job. Then he completed 12 of 15 passes for 186 yards and three touchdowns, which perhaps made releasing him more difficult.
The Browns had four quarterbacks and room for three. By Sunday, the Browns placed him on injured reserve with a designation to return. He must miss at least four games, but he does not count against the active roster.
The injury may be completely legitimate. Gabriel reportedly hurt his back during the game, and there is no evidence the Browns fabricated anything. But injuries can also create opportunistic roster solutions. Both can be true.
The Browns no longer had to choose between Gabriel, the former third-round pick who performed well in the finale, and Green, the rookie with the size, speed and physical upside this coaching staff clearly values. They retained both without sacrificing a roster spot at another position or exposing either quarterback to waivers.
The NFL is filled with coincidences around cutdown weekend. This one worked perfectly for the Browns.
It’s the latest unusual turn for Gabriel, who has spent the past 16 months trapped in everyone else’s story.
The Browns drafted him with the No. 94 pick last year after one of the most productive careers in college football history. Gabriel tied the FBS record with 155 touchdown passes, finished second in career passing yards and started more games than any quarterback in major college history.
Under normal circumstances, a third-round quarterback with that resume would have arrived as an intriguing developmental prospect.
Gabriel received about 24 hours.
Then the Browns drafted Sanders two rounds later, and Gabriel became the answer to an entirely different question: Why did the Browns take him before Shedeur?
The Curious Case of Dillon Gabriel is fascinating because selecting him in the third round was an organizational decision aimed at developing a backup quarterback. The front office and coaching staff were aligned in believing he could be a long-term backup, which raises a multitude of questions about a bad team with plenty of holes spending valuable draft capital on a quarterback unanimously believed to have the ceiling of being a career backup.
Nevertheless, the Browns have struggled for generations to develop any sort of quarterback, and they loved the way Gabriel saw and thought the game. He wasn’t supposed to play last year because the Browns had two veterans in front of him: Joe Flacco and Kenny Pickett.
But this is Cleveland, and it’s only a matter of time before the Browns go full Browns, which they did the day after drafting Gabriel when they drafted Sanders. Suddenly, there was a new plan, and Gabriel’s place in it was hard to track.
It didn’t matter that he had nothing to do with where either player was selected. Fans viewed him as the quarterback standing in Sanders’ way.
Gabriel nevertheless won the backup job behind Flacco. By the fifth game of the season, he became the starter.
He went 1-5 in six starts. He was leading at halftime of the Ravens game when he left with a concussion. He threw seven touchdown passes against only two interceptions, but he completed only 59.5 percent of his passes and struggled driving the ball down the field and creating explosive plays. Regardless of how he sees the game, he lacks the physical tools to be a difference-maker at the position.
As a cheap backup, Gabriel is serviceable in small doses. He isn’t a disaster, as he was painted at times last season. He generally protects the football and can operate an offense effectively. He just doesn’t do much to elevate it.
Gabriel hasn’t started a game since the concussion.
Sanders replaced him, struggled badly that evening, then won in Las Vegas the following week while Gabriel remained in the concussion protocol. The Browns initially indicated Gabriel would return as the starter when healthy. Sanders kept the job instead.
The concussion may have changed the direction of Gabriel’s career, showing how quickly opportunities can appear and disappear for young quarterbacks without the protection of a massive contract or premium draft status.
By the time Gabriel returned this summer, the coaching staff had been fired. Todd Monken inherited him rather than chose him. Watson returned from two Achilles surgeries. Sanders entered camp with a chance to start. The Browns drafted Green, whose 6-foot-6 frame and rare athleticism make him a fascinating developmental project.
Every other quarterback represented something larger.
Watson represented the Browns’ lingering desperation to salvage their franchise-altering gamble. Sanders represented celebrity, fan support and the possibility of something more. Green represented physical traits you can’t teach.
Gabriel represented last year.
He wasn’t included in the real starting competition. By the final preseason game, he was playing merely to retain his place in the organization. Then he produced his best performance as a Brown.
Gabriel was accurate. He created downfield plays. He threw three touchdowns in the first half and forced the Browns to reconsider how easily they could move on from him.
Monken made clear afterward that the performance changed nothing at the top of the depth chart. Watson remained the starter. Sanders remained the backup. All Gabriel did was complicate the bottom.
Then came the back injury and the injured-reserve designation. Whether by misfortune, convenient roster management or some combination of the two, the Browns opted to kick the football down the road at least a month before they have to make any decisions.
Gabriel pays a price for the arrangement. He cannot practice or play for at least four weeks. Green will receive the developmental work as the third quarterback. While Gabriel rehabilitates, the Browns will learn more about everyone else in the room.
By October, circumstances may decide his future again. Watson could struggle or get hurt. Sanders could play. Green could develop. Another team could need a quarterback. The Browns might activate Gabriel, trade him or leave him waiting.
That is the strange part of his story. Gabriel has started six NFL games, handled every demotion professionally and performed well when his roster spot appeared to depend on it. Yet the Browns still haven’t reached a firm conclusion about him.
They don’t believe in him enough to play him. They don’t doubt him enough to release him.
So they placed him in the spot that truly fits his Cleveland career — neither part of the present nor free to pursue a future elsewhere.
Still here. Still waiting.
Not quite good enough to be chosen.

full_text:
Pat Surtain II leads one of football's most imposing defenses. Emilee Chinn / Getty Images
There’s just something about those Denver Broncos defenses. The “Orange Crush” of the late 1970s rocked pro football with its 3-4 scheme. The “No Fly Zone” brought home a championship in 2015. Mile High has been defined by the likes of Karl Mecklenburg and Champ Bailey, bellows of “ in-com-plete! ” through the thinning air.
Denver enters 2026 with yet another havoc-wreaking D. Vance Joseph’s group notched an absurd 68 sacks last year, 11 more than the No. 2 pass rush. It ranked second in yards allowed and third in points allowed, too. Expect a similar level of dominance with Zach Allen on the line, Nik Bonitto off the edge and Pat Surtain II in the secondary.
The other side of the ball should continue to improve under mastermind Sean Payton and new offensive coordinator Davis Webb . J.K. Dobbins and RJ Harvey front a versatile backfield. Jaylen Waddle joins Troy Franklin and Courtland Sutton to fill out the receiving room. And the offensive line has a first-team All-Pro mauler in Garett Bolles.
It’ll all come down to Bo Nix, though. Denver’s quarterback showed resolve throughout his second season. His performance in the AFC divisional round was inspired … and his subsequent injury became a “ where were you when? ” moment.
This hyped Broncos campaign begins under the spotlight with a Week 1 “Monday Night Football” trip to the Kansas City Chiefs, a battle between two AFC West contenders. There are two other primetime spots in the first six weeks, as well as national TV games on Black Friday and Christmas.
Keep up with all the news fit to type by following the Broncos on The Athletic. Writer Nick Kosmider is one of the best on the beat.
All times listed below are ET.
The most expansive option for live game coverage is a multichannel plan. That includes streamers like Fubo, Sling TV and YouTube TV, or more traditional providers like DirecTV, Dish and Xfinity. We lay out cord-cutting alternatives for each NFL media partner down below, but there’s a certain peace of mind to the consolidation of pay television.
Main window: Sunday afternoon (in-market fans)
Playoffs: 1 wild-card game, 1 divisional game, AFC Championship Game
Each week, CBS carries games across two Sunday kickoff slots: one at 1 p.m., and another at 4:05 p.m. or the national window at 4:25 p.m. There will be 10 nationwide Sunday doubleheaders this year on CBS. Broadcasts are set by region when there are multiple offerings in a spot.
It’s not a clean split, but CBS is known as the primary home of the AFC. The network’s theme music is a certified slapper.
Its main pregame show, “The NFL Today,” adds one-time Broncos quarterback Russell Wilson and fellow recent retiree Kyle Long to its studio crew. CBS announcers include Jim Nantz and Ian Eagle, while the color commentary rotation stars JJ Watt.
What you’ll need to watch: A pay TV package, or an indoor TV antenna for free over-the-air viewing. Local CBS games also stream on Paramount+.
Main window: Sunday afternoon (in-market fans)
Playoffs: 1 wild-card game, 1 divisional game, NFC Championship Game
Like CBS, Fox splits Sunday afternoons between early 1 p.m. action and later 4:05/4:25 p.m. matchups. Its centerpiece is branded as “America’s Game of the Week.” Unlike CBS, Fox has a dancing robot named Cleatus . It’s the nominal network for the NFC as well.
Kevin Burkhardt, Joe Davis and Adam Amin are the lead play-by-play voices. Burkhardt pairs with Tom Brady, while Davis calls games alongside Greg Olsen. Amin is partnered with newcomer Drew Brees, who is fresh off his Pro Football Hall of Fame induction. Some Spanish-language broadcasts are available on Fox Deportes.
What you’ll need to watch: A pay TV package, or an antenna for free over-the-air viewing. Local Fox games also stream on Fox One.
Main window: Sunday afternoon (out-of-market fans)
These two are the access points for all non-national matchups that aren’t on regional CBS or Fox.
NFL Sunday Ticket has full games. It’s exclusive to YouTube and YouTube TV. Those without a YouTube TV plan can still get NFL Sunday Ticket as a primetime channel through the standard YouTube app.
RedZone is the whip-around program that jumps around the slate to cover scoring drives. This is the place for Scott Hanson , “the witching hour” and chaotic octobox split screens. It can be added to NFL Sunday Ticket, and it’s included on some high-end pay TV sports plans.
RedZone also lives on NFL+ Premium, which can be bundled with the ESPN Unlimited plan.
What you’ll need to watch: An NFL Sunday Ticket subscription through YouTube TV or the YouTube app; NFL RedZone access through select pay TV packages, ESPN Unlimited or NFL+ Premium.
Playoffs: 2 wild-card games, 1 divisional game
This is the faithful home of “Sunday Night Football” each weekend. And because everything has to be confusing, the NBC lineup opens with a Wednesday night season premiere. At least SNF has a consistent 8:20 p.m. start time.
Mike Tirico and Cris Collinsworth are in the booth, with Melissa Stark reporting from the sidelines. Carrie Underwood sings about waiting all day for Sunday night . NBC’s “Football Night in America” pregame show brings on longtime head coach Mike Tomlin. Telemundo has the telecasts in Spanish.
The network has two extra Saturday offerings for Week 17. One is exclusive to Peacock, and both matchups will be announced later in the season. The same goes for NBC’s Week 18 regular-season finale.
“Sunday Night Football” is subject to flex scheduling — games can be swapped in and out of the window twice between Weeks 5-10 and any time from Weeks 11-17. This allows executives to pick games with greater playoff implications, though it leaves the actual ticket holders in a bind.
What you’ll need to watch: A pay TV package, or an antenna for free over-the-air viewing, or a Peacock account with the live sports plan.
Playoffs: 1 wild-card game, 1 divisional game, Super Bowl LXI
The Disney networks combine to cover 17 “Monday Night Football” games. Ten of those are on both ABC and ESPN, with another seven exclusive to the latter. The oft-maligned “Monday Night Football” doubleheader is now a thing of the past.
MNF kickoffs have 8:15 p.m. starts, and their schedule flexes can happen any time in Weeks 12-17. The two Saturday ABC/ESPN matchups in Week 18 will be set as the postseason picture sharpens.
ESPN is preparing for its first Super Bowl broadcast ever on Feb. 14, 2027. It will be simulcast on ABC.
Joe Buck handles play-by-play for MNF. He’s joined by analyst Troy Aikman, plus the sideline duo of Lisa Salters and Laura Rutledge. Spanish-language airings can be found on ESPN Deportes. For 12 regular-season games and the Super Bowl, ESPN2 offers an alternate “ManningCast,” in which Super Bowl 50 champ Peyton Manning (and his brother Eli) watch the games with famous fans. Guests have ranged from Bill Belichick to Lil Wayne .
What you’ll need to watch: A pay TV package, or an antenna for ABC, or an ESPN Unlimited account.
Main window: Thursday night
Playoffs: 1 wild-card game
Most weeks begin with “Thursday Night Football,” which kicks off at 8:15 p.m. Those games are behind the Prime paywall, but they’re free over the air in the participants’ home markets. Flex rules around TNF are a bit less hectic, with two allotments between Weeks 13-17.
Despite it not being on a Thursday, this is also where you can find the Broncos’ visit to the Pittsburgh Steelers on Black Friday. It starts at 3 p.m. and not in the usual primetime window.
Thursdays are called by Al Michaels and Kirk Herbstreit, with Kaylee Hartung on sideline duty. Herbstreit loves dogs ; Michaels hates vegetables . Prime has Spanish-language coverage and advanced stat broadcast options within its app. Among the pregame and postgame personalities are former All-Pros Tony Gonzalez, Richard Sherman and Andrew Whitworth.
What you’ll need to watch: Amazon Prime. TNF is also free on Twitch…

Caleb Williams enters Year 3 for the Chicago Bears as reigning NFC North champions. Patrick McDermott / Getty Images
Last season, the Chicago Bears smashed their 7.5-win total with an 11-6 run to their first NFC North title since 2018. To start this season, they’re sitting third on the list of odds to win the division.
Their +305 odds give them a 23 percent implied probability to defend their crown, so they’re not far behind the Detroit Lions at +175 (33 percent) — or the Green Bay Packers at +240 (27 percent).
My model forecasts a similarly close race that actually positions the Bears slightly ahead of the Packers. Let’s run through his model’s projections and dive into how close it could really be between the Bears and Lions.
The Bears are a tricky team to project heading into the season.
First and foremost, they won seven one-score games last year, which leads me to believe that will regress a little bit. The defense also leaves something to be desired after finishing last season 30th in Expected Points Added (EPA) per play when excluding turnovers. And while I believe coach Ben Johnson is one of the best offensive minds in football, and that being paired with Caleb Williams for another season should take the offense to a new level, how Williams’ development in Year 3 will be the key to their season.
The clearest reason the Bears aren’t favored to win the division, though, is because of their schedule. They play the toughest schedule in the NFC North by a decent margin, the 19th-toughest in the league. An average team would be expected to win 8.5 of those games. By comparison, the Lions play the third-easiest schedule, which an average team would be expected to win nine of those games.
The Lions also grade out as the better team in my model. The Bears have the higher upside on offense, but the Lions have the safer floor. Jared Goff, Jahmyr Gibbs and Amon-Ra St. Brown coupled with a re-tooled offensive line is a good place to start. The defense does give me some pause — especially with defensive backs Brian Branch and Kerby Joseph not able to suit up for at least the first month of the season — but their front seven led by Aidan Hutchinson and Jack Campbell gives the Lions the edge there, too.
Still, these teams aren’t separated by much. In fact, on a neutral field, my model would favor the Lions by less than a half-point. It’s close, but every factor has to be taken into account when running season simulations, and the question of how Williams develops coupled with the Lions’ favorable schedule is enough to give Detroit the lead in my projections.

full_text:
Kyle Long, despite his best efforts, never played a snap for the Chiefs after his unretirement. Andrew Mather / Kansas City Chiefs via Associated Press
Kyle Long walked out of Raymond James Stadium in Tampa on a cool February night in 2021 when the realization hit him.
One year removed from his retirement as an offensive lineman for the Chicago Bears, Long was now building a media career at CBS Sports and had just finished covering his first Super Bowl. He strolled the parking lot with Pro Football Hall of Fame coach Bill Cowher, his now-colleague, the chaos from the day slowly dissipating around them. But there was one aspect of the game Long couldn’t get out of his head.
He turned to Cowher: “Maybe I’m a guy that can help Patrick Mahomes.”
The Tampa Bay Buccaneers battered the Kansas City Chiefs star quarterback in their 31-9 Super Bowl 55 win that day. Behind a makeshift offensive line, Mahomes was sacked three times and was pressured on 29 of his 56 dropbacks, the most of any quarterback in Super Bowl history. For the first time as a pro, Mahomes lost a game by double digits, and his team never scored a touchdown.
Watching this, with a press pass on instead of pads, left Long infuriated. The next day, he sent Mahomes a message.
“There should have been a million offensive linemen that called him and said, whatever you need, I’ll do it in jeans and boots,” Long said in a conversation with The Athletic this summer. “That’s pretty much what the message was that I sent him. And he was like, get a hold of Andy (Reid), let’s make this thing happen.”
One month later, Long signed with the Chiefs. Retirement postponed.
Nothing beats an underdog story. But the story of unretirement comes pretty close, a narrative complete with anticipation, pressure and perseverance. This week, three-time NFL Defensive Player of the Year Aaron Donald announced his return to the Los Angeles Rams more than two years after he retired from football. Donald, 35, makes a Rams roster that was already the Super Bowl favorite look invincible . That is, if he can return to the form that made him a future Hall of Famer in the first place.
Players coming back, despite their ages or injuries, can humanize even the biggest stars. Michael Jordan was already a three-time NBA champion when he retired to try his hand in baseball. Then he said, “I’m back,” and embarked on another NBA three-peat. Michael Phelps won 18 Olympic gold medals when he retired after the 2012 Games; he came back and won five more in 2016.
Some might say these stars should be satisfied. Let them ride off into the sunset and make room for the next generation. But for athletes wired on competitive drive, there comes a time when more than medals, rings or accolades are on the line. It gets personal.
Lindsey Vonn returned to competitive skiing at 40 in the lead-up to the 2026 Winter Olympics, citing a deep love for the sport, speed and competition. She made it to Cortina d’Ampezzo, but crashed during her downhill run and was airlifted out with a devastating injury. This summer, tennis great Serena Williams returned to the singles court at Wimbledon after almost four years away, where she lost in the first round and injured her knee. At 44 years old, she’s set to return to the U.S. Open this month , competing in doubles with her sister Venus, even if Wimbledon didn’t go her way.
In football, returning from retirement comes with added challenges. The physicality of the game puts players on tight timelines, and any extended period away only makes it harder to get back into game shape.
Tight end Rob Gronkowski came out of a one-year retirement to join his old teammate Tom Brady in Tampa Bay in 2020, winning that ring that Long watched from the crowd. Two years later, Brady announced his own retirement, only to backtrack 40 days later and return for one final season at 45 years old, becoming the oldest quarterback to start and win a game.
Quarterback Brett Favre had an even longer grapple with retirement. Favre first retired after the 2007 season with the Green Bay Packers and then following the 2008 season with the New York Jets. He returned to the field both times.
“I don’t know for me if it’s ever easy,” Favre told reporters , announcing his official retirement after the 2010 season with the Minnesota Vikings. “I’m sure throughout this year the comment has been made that, ‘We’ll wait and see in August or September,’ and that’s fine. It’s time. I’m OK with it.”
Just as recently as 2025, the Indianapolis Colts called up 44-year-old Philip Rivers to revitalize their injury-riddled quarterback room, five years removed from Rivers’ last snap.
So, what fuels a comeback? And how does a player prepare for a return to the gridiron? Each athlete’s motivation is unique. But across interviews with multiple NFL players, one thing became clear: a desire to forgo the second-guessing for a second chance, no matter how it ends up.
“I left with a little bit of almost a bad taste in my mouth the first time I retired just because (I thought): Was this the right decision? Was it not? I was just so iffy on it,” said former linebacker Kyle Emanuel, who retired after the 2019 season with the Los Angeles Chargers and rejoined the league one year later. “The fact that I was able to come back, get another year, regardless if it went the way I envisioned or not, I think it was huge for me.”
Tight end Darren Waller was halfway into his 2023 season with the New York Giants when he began to seriously consider retirement. He contemplated his decision in the months following that season, telling The Athletic ’s Dan Duggan at the time: “It’s really the idea of signing up for another journey. It’s tough, it’s long, it requires a lot. And if you’re not fully bought into every single thing of the process, it’s going to be tough.”
Multiple athletes shared the same sentiment. Why return to the game if you can’t — mentally, physically, emotionally — give it your all? Reflecting this summer, Waller reiterated the pressure felt during an NFL season.
“The game’s fast. You’re moving from one thing to the next,” he said. “Your nervous system’s always heightened because you’ve got to be ready for so much pressure, stress, pain, high highs. So, it was a big adjustment for me to slow my life down the way that I had to and needed to.”
Waller announced his retirement in June 2023 at 31. Injuries caused him to miss 19 games over his last three years. Waller also battled a drug and alcohol addiction early in his career, and he was suspended the entire 2017 season for violating the NFL’s substance abuse policy. But no factor played a more impactful role in Waller’s decision to step away than his desire to look inward.
“This life that looks good on paper and is — by all means — successful by the common American definition of success. But it’s like, it doesn’t feel right or feel aligned within me,” Waller said. “Everybody would choose my life from the outside looking in, but I am not necessarily choosing my life for myself. So what needs to change? I feel like that required me to remove myself from performing to slow everything down, strip a lot of things away and just walk through that process.”
Emanuel, the linebacker who retired after four seasons with the Chargers, was almost moved to tears sitting at his locker after his team’s 2019 divisional-round loss to the New England Patriots, thinking: “Was that my last game?” For a former fifth-round pick whose contract had just expired, retirement felt like something always lurking in his rearview mirror.
“You hear so much when you’re in the NFL: It’s short-lived. You just never know. Injuries happen. You get cut,” Emanuel said. “I didn’t really know what I wanted to do next. That part of it was always on my mind, actually.”
As Long remembers it, retirement wasn’t a common topic discussed between teammates in the locker room. It silently crept around as what Long called the “Grim Reaper,” usually someone from the scouting or…

full_text:
Andrew Van Ginkel is healthy and ready for another productive season, but the Vikings would benefit from additional depth at edge rusher. Elsa / Getty Images
Quarterbacks dominated the early analysis in the aftermath of the Minnesota Vikings naming their initial 53-man roster . But there are other position groups that still warrant attention.
Minnesota currently has about $21 million in cap space. In the past, the team pushed some of that money forward for future seasons, but the focus on winning — and doing it sooner rather than later — suggests the Vikings are likely to use it this season.
If the Vikings splurge to add talent to the roster before the Week 1 game against the Green Bay Packers, where could they look, and who could they target?
Here is a breakdown of potential moves at four non-quarterback positions:
Trading Jonathan Greenard brought attention to this position months ago. The move added urgency to 2024 first-round pick Dallas Turner’s development and made Andrew Van Ginkel staying healthy much more vital.
Turner’s training camp performance has inspired internal optimism. Van Ginkel’s availability has, too. But depth continues to be an important question, and Sunday’s news tossed gasoline on the fire.
Tyler Batty, an undrafted, second-year player from BYU, tore his ACL in the team’s final preseason game against the Denver Broncos. The season-ending injury left the team with just four edge rushers on its initial 53-man roster. Former undrafted players Chaz Chambliss and Bo Richter offer versatility and special teams value, but neither has the edge-setting presence to fill in for Turner or Van Ginkel.
There are only so many options available for the Vikings. They passed on plucking a player from the waiver wire, although rosters will still be in flux in the ensuing days. Free agency is another potential avenue. However, some of the best candidates in that pool — such as veteran Jadeveon Clowney — signed elsewhere.
There are still some productive players out there. Kyle Van Noy played for defensive coordinator Brian Flores in 2020 and is still unsigned. Free agents Haason Reddick and Leonard Floyd posted higher pressure rates than Van Noy last season, and both remain on the market.
The flexibility of current Vikings defenders Eric Wilson, Jake Golday and Ty Ingram-Dawkins provides short-term cover. But Minnesota would raise its defensive floor by adding another accomplished player at the position.
The night before training camp began, the Vikings signed veteran defender Jamal Adams. They viewed him as a potential fixer in different packages. His blitzing ability and ruggedness near the line of scrimmage would allow them to maintain much of their defensive structure. (That was previously in jeopardy with Josh Metellus making a temporary shift to play in the deeper parts of the field.)
Adams’ torn quad threw a wrench in the Vikings’ plans. Without him, Minnesota found itself back in the same spot. Fourth-year safety Jay Ward flashed in the preseason. Undrafted rookie Jacob Thomas wowed coaches with his acumen. Asking both to play significant snaps as safeties Theo Jackson and Jakobe Thomas rehabbed their way back from injury was lofty. Then Jacob Thomas sprained his ankle in Friday’s preseason finale.
Adding to the uncertainty is the situation of legendary safety Harrison Smith. Last week, coach Kevin O’Connell said that Smith had been in contact. The Vikings have left the door open for Smith, 37, to return if he felt the itch. That’s the first hurdle. The second is what a new contract could look like.
Minnesota paid Smith $10.7 million in 2025, according to Over The Cap. He is a year older, but the Vikings’ need at safety gives him leverage. His re-signing would allow Metellus to return to his optimal position in the box or as a slot defender. It would also allow Smith to return to orchestrating Flores’ pre-snap checks, a critical component of countering opposing offenses in real time.
Keeping four tight ends seemed realistic. The Vikings hope for a resurgence from T.J. Hockenson this season, and Josh Oliver retains his role as a run blocker who can dictate defensive personnel groupings.
There is some ambiguity, however, over the roles of fellow tight ends Ben Yurosek and Gavin Bartholomew, both of whom are on the 53-man. Yurosek plays a significant role on special teams. Bartholomew, a 2025 sixth-round pick who missed his entire rookie season with a back injury, emerged with an impressive showing in training camp. He caught five passes for 26 yards in the final preseason game against the Broncos. The showing solidified his standing as worthy of a roster spot.
Now, the only impediment to both young tight ends staying active would be the addition of a veteran tight end capable of playing meaningful offensive snaps.
Initial rosters are subject to change. The Vikings telegraphed their upcoming maneuvers by keeping only eight offensive linemen. The starting five players are healthy and prepared, but the backup circumstances warranted deeper questioning.
So Minnesota claimed two players off waivers Monday: guard Trevor Keegan, formerly of the Dallas Cowboys, and center Nick Samac, previously of the Carolina Panthers. Each played more than 100 snaps in the preseason and caught the attention of evaluators.
Keegan thrives as a physical run blocker, while Samac is a capable former seventh-round pick of the Baltimore Ravens. They join Ryan Van Demark, Caleb Tiernan and Joe Huber as backups on the O-line. How quickly Samac can get up to speed with O’Connell’s complex system could dictate whether the Vikings will have confidence turning to him, particularly with backup center Michael Jurgens on injured reserve with an undisclosed injury.
Most importantly, these inclusions address the need up front.

They set their initial 53-man roster late on Sunday. And on Monday, they nabbed two players off waivers, selecting tight end Cameron Latu and linebacker Darius Muas
full_text:
The Patriots are likely to be relying heavily on rookie Gabe Jacas to help with the team's lackluster pass rush. Maddie Meyer / Getty Images
The New England Patriots have spent the last few days tweaking their roster. They added backup running back Corey Kiner and backup offensive tackle Walter Rouse via late-round draft-pick trades. They set their initial 53-man roster late on Sunday. And on Monday, they nabbed two players off waivers, selecting tight end Cameron Latu and linebacker Darius Muasau for additional depth.
That helps answer the most pertinent questions about the roster. But plenty of questions remain about the state of the Patriots with the opener in Seattle a little over a week away. Today, let’s look at the lingering questions still facing the franchise.
Last season, following injuries to defensive linemen Harold Landry and Milton Williams, now-defensive coordinator Zak Kuhr ramped up his blitz percentage in an attempt to make up for their losses. In the first half of last season, the Patriots ranked 21st in blitz percentage. In the second half, they ranked fifth.
The hope from coaches this offseason was that they wouldn’t have to play that way again — that they’d be able to create a more consistent pass rush with their front four.
But that’s looking unlikely. Landry is on the PUP list, which means he’ll miss at least the first four games. Rookie second-round pick Gabe Jacas is behind schedule after missing summer practices. Offseason signing Dre’Mont Jones isn’t a pure pass rusher. Plenty is already on the shoulders of Elijah Ponder, who went undrafted last year.
That leaves edge rusher, without question, as the team’s weakest position.
Part of the hope here lies with Christian Barmore. Last season, Barmore ranked 11th in the league among defensive tackles in Pro Football Focus’ win rate and 29th among defensive linemen in pressure rate. Yet that led to just two sacks, which is probably an anomaly. If Barmore repeats (or improves on) that level of play, he should get more than a couple sacks, which would help the defense significantly.
But as for a pass rush off the edge, there aren’t a lot of reasons for hope. That’s part of why it won’t be a surprise if Kuhr again leans on the blitz, at least early in the season, even if that puts a lot of pressure on the secondary.
It’s not often we get this close to the start of the season without a definitive answer here. And it’s important because kick returns were one of the few areas in which the Patriots weren’t an above-average team last season.
A year ago, they ranked 19th in the league in yards per kickoff and 18th in average starting field position off kickoffs.
The best guess is that Kyle Williams probably starts off returning kicks to flex his 4.4-second 40-yard speed. But Kiner, their new No. 3 running back, has returned kicks before and could factor into that role, too, or play next to Williams there. Efton Chism would be the third option for this spot, but his lack of straight-line speed (4.71-second 40) does show up in this area.
While the rest of the league predominantly uses 11 personnel (with three wide receivers), the Pats ranked 24th in usage of that grouping last season.
The thought entering this offseason was that they’d lean more into 12 personnel, taking advantage of multiple tight ends on the field at the same time. But that’s in question now that Julian Hill is out for the season and rookie Eli Raridon is the No. 2 option at the position.
The guess here is the Patriots will use a relatively high amount of 21 personnel with two running backs on the field. Last season, they ranked fifth in the league in 21 usage. That could even go up this season now that they have a reliable fullback in Reggie Gilliam.
Plus, given the additions of A.J. Brown and Romeo Doubs and their depth at wide receiver, it wouldn’t be a surprise if this were the first season since 2022 that New England ranked in the top half of the league in 11 personnel usage.
As a general rule of thumb, it’s not a great sign that the team felt the need to trade for depth at offensive tackle on Sunday, even though the Patriots used their first-round pick on a player (Caleb Lomu) who was supposed to provide depth at the position.
Marcus Bryant seemed to beat out Lomu for the swing tackle job before suffering an injury that will keep him out for at least four games. Then the team traded for Rouse even though Lomu and Dametrious Crownover were both already on the roster.
All of this raises the question: If Will Campbell or Morgan Moses were to get hurt, would the Patriots turn to their first-round pick or a player they just traded for?
Of course, this is the big one. And what more needs to be said?
When Devon Witherspoon became the highest-paid cornerback in NFL history, a blueprint was provided for how to get a Gonzalez deal done. That there is no deal yet suggests there are quite a few hang-ups.
The unofficial deadline for an extension is the Sept. 9 opener. So, about one week remains for the two sides to reach a deal.

summary:

full_text:
Aaron Glenn is looking at a turnaround in 2026, and Garrett Wilson will be a big part of it. Adam Hunger / Associated Press
FLORHAM PARK, N.J. — The New York Jets are under construction.
That’s true in a literal sense. Renovations at the team’s facility are currently underway to upgrade the team’s weight room, one year after Jets owner Woody Johnson invested in locker room upgrades.
It’s also true in the figurative sense. Head coach Aaron Glenn has taken on some renovations of his own. He fired half his coaching staff, took over play-calling on defense and worked with general manager Darren Mougey to add veterans and leaders on both sides of the ball that were missing during last season’s 3-14 finish.
Expectations for this year’s Jets team are low outside of Florham Park. The players know it. Glenn can feel it too. Across the NFL on Sunday, rosters were trimmed from 90 to 53 players. The majority of the players who practiced Monday will be the ones who determine if the Jets can overcome the overwhelming noise that people view them as one of the worst teams in the NFL. It’s an uphill battle many coaches before Glenn have tried to overcome.
“You get used to hearing so many opinions, so much outside noise that a lot of teams (those people) don’t really know what’s going on, on the inside,” Glenn said Monday. “We’re doing everything we can to change the perception of how people see this organization, how people see the coaches, how people see this team. We’re going to continue to work at that, and I think from my perspective it’s: How do I improve as a coach? That’s been documented. How do we improve as a team, how do we get the right players and how do we go through training camp to make sure our guys are physically and emotionally ready for Week 1? I just want everyone outside this building to understand that, man, we’re working our ass off to make sure we do that. We never said it’s going to be easy.”
It never is. Are the Jets in the right position to exceed expectations? How should they feel about Geno Smith at quarterback and other key pieces on the roster?
Here are some things I’m seeing with the Jets coming out of training camp.
Every year, I track all of the starting quarterback’s throws during team drills — and the throws of any notable backups. That includes who the quarterback throws to. It’s an inexact science and an unofficial tally (sometimes we are positioned at an angle that makes it challenging to pinpoint exactly who was targeted on every throw), but it is a fun and educational exercise. It can be predictive in some ways to figure out where all the pass catchers fall in the pecking order when the season comes, especially for those who got more reps with the top quarterback.
A few years ago, a former Jets staffer told me they also track throws in camp, and that many teams do as well.
That gets us to this year’s QB1: Smith. If I were to grade how he looked this summer, I’d probably land somewhere in the B/B-plus range. He had some practices when he couldn’t miss (11-for-11 on Aug. 1, 14-for-18 on Aug. 18 and 16-for-19 on Aug. 25). He also had some bad days, especially in the joint practices against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers.
Overall, I would say there was more good than bad. His arm talent is obvious, his teammates seem to like him, and there’s good reason to think the Jets offense should show significant improvement after last year’s mess. The Smith journey can be a roller coaster, but he’s a perfectly capable quarterback when he’s kept clean.
As for the numbers: My final tally was 113 completions on 167 attempts (67.6 percent) with 12 touchdowns and four interceptions. I did miss two practices and didn’t include stats from seven-on-seven drills.
As for who he targeted the most often, Garrett Wilson was, unsurprisingly, his favorite receiver — 27 catches on 42 targets with three touchdowns — but Adonai Mitchell wasn’t far behind. I’d argue Smith’s chemistry with Mitchell (18 catches on 27 targets with three touchdowns) was even better than with Wilson.
Isaiah Williams (13 catches on 19 targets, three touchdowns) and tight end Mason Taylor (17 catches on 19 targets, two touchdowns) were the next-most targeted pass catchers, with rookie receiver Omar Cooper Jr. (eight catches on 15 targets, one touchdown) just behind them. Cooper took some time to get going but came on strong at the end of camp.
In March, Glenn cited Taylor as someone he expected to take a leap, and it’s hard to argue with that after watching how he performed during camp. Williams also played his way into a legitimate role on offense as a slot and gadget receiver.
I didn’t record very many targets to the running backs throughout the summer, just three to Breece Hall and four to Braelon Allen from Smith. I’m not sure if that’s an indication of what’s to come, but it’s worth noting.
But if Smith finished the 2026 season completing 67 percent of his passes with a 3:1 touchdown ratio, the Jets would be ecstatic.
It became clear early in training camp that neither Brady Cook or Bailey Zappe were seriously pushing Cade Klubnik for the No. 2 job. Klubnik got every rep as the QB2 — and Cook and Zappe, as expected, were waived Sunday. (Cook was claimed off waivers by the Miami Dolphins.)
The Jets didn’t add any new quarterbacks via waiver claim, and Glenn confirmed Monday that Klubnik will be Smith’s backup. “It’s just the confidence in how he operates and what he’s done in practice, what he’s done in the games,” Glenn said. “I don’t think anybody said there won’t be hiccups. He’s a rookie, he’s always learning, but he’s a very intelligent guy. We’re proud that we have him.”
He turned the ball over a decent amount and wasn’t always perfect, but I thought overall Klubnik was fine. He showed impressive poise for a rookie in his preseason debut, and he made some impressive throws in camp, though he clearly doesn’t have arm talent approaching the level of Smith. He took a step back in his last two preseason games, especially on an interception he threw against the New York Giants.
As for the final tally — not counting preseason games — I had Klubnik completing 74 of 118 passes (62.7 percent) for nine touchdowns and seven interceptions. In the three preseason games, Klubnik was 21 of 34 (61.7 percent) for 197 yards, zero touchdowns and one interception, adding 22 yards on two carries.
His No. 1 target in training camp: Tight end Jelani Woods, who caught 10 of 13 targets from Klubnik (Woods also caught three of six targets from Smith) and scored two touchdowns. Jeremy Ruckert caught all eight of his passes from Klubnik and eight of nine from Smith. Williams (nine catches on 12 targets) and Tim Patrick (five catches on 11 targets) were Klubnik’s top wide receiver targets.
Here’s how I’d rank the Jets’ top-10 players based on what I saw in training camp:
1. WR Garrett Wilson: He’s still clearly their most talented player and in line for a huge season if Smith can perform as even a league-average quarterback.
2. S Minkah Fitzpatrick: He does not look like he’s lost a step. Fitzpatrick made plays all over the field all summer.
3. OT Armand Membou: He had some dominant stretches of camp and looks ready for a jump.
4. LB Demario Davis: A steady, stable veteran and leader who still has plenty left in the tank.
5. OLB David Bailey: He looks ready to make an instant impact — even more than anyone could’ve reasonably expected. I was tempted to rank him higher.
6. RB Breece Hall: He ran the ball extremely well all summer before a groin injury.
7. QB Geno Smith: See above.
8. P Austin McNamara: They call him “the sniper” for a reason.
9. OLB Kingsley Enagbare: A pleasant surprise, he’s clearly ahead of Will McDonald and took advantage of Joe Ossai’s injury.
10. TE Mason Taylor: He looks ready to take a real leap forward with some improved quarterback play.
Left tackle Olu Fashanu and Mitchell have a case here, as does Joe Tippmann. T’Vondre Sweat might have made it onto the list if he’d practiced…

title: How to watch the 2026 Pittsburgh Steelers: A TV guide for Terrible Towel wavers The Steelers are going for their third AFC North title of the 2020s. Here's a look at their schedule and the cost to watch their games. Steven Louis Goldstein 1

full_text:
DK Metcalf returns as WR1 for the AFC North champions. Joe Sargent / Getty Images
According to the United States Census Bureau, Pittsburgh ranks 27th in metro area population. But of far greater importance, no team has more Super Bowl rings in the NFL record books than the Pittsburgh Steelers.
The Steelers’ six Lombardi Trophies are matched only by the New England Patriots. While New England did all of its damage in the Tom Brady/Bill Belichick era, Pittsburgh has sustained its excellence across several iterations. Chuck Noll earned four championships with the likes of Terry Bradshaw, Franco Harris and the “Steel Curtain” defense. Bill Cowher broke through with Super Bowl XL MVP Hines Ward. And Mike Tomlin won it all thanks to Santonio Holmes’ all-time great grab .
The quest for No. 7 begins this September. New head coach Mike McCarthy reunites with Aaron Rodgers. DK Metcalf, Michael Pittman Jr. and Germie Bernard form a remade receiver room. The talented defense includes veterans T.J. Watt, Cameron Heyward, Alex Highsmith and Jalen Ramsey.
Pittsburgh takes the field as the reigning AFC North champ, with a schedule that reflects its national intrigue. The Steelers are slated for four traditional primetime matchups, plus an inaugural Paris game versus the New Orleans Saints and a Black ( and Yellow ) Friday special against the Denver Broncos. To stay up to date, follow the team on The Athletic and senior writer Mike DeFabo on the beat.
All times listed below are ET.
The most expansive option for live game coverage is a multichannel plan. That includes streamers like Fubo, Sling TV and YouTube TV, or more traditional providers like DirecTV, Dish and Xfinity. We lay out cord-cutting alternatives for each NFL media partner down below, but there’s a certain peace of mind to the consolidation of pay television.
Main window: Sunday afternoon (in-market fans)
Playoffs: 1 wild-card game, 1 divisional game, AFC Championship Game
Each week, CBS carries games across two Sunday kickoff slots: one at 1 p.m., and another at 4:05 p.m. or the national window at 4:25 p.m. There will be 10 nationwide Sunday doubleheaders this year on CBS. Broadcasts are set by region when there are multiple offerings in a spot.
It’s not a clean split, but CBS is known as the primary home of the AFC. The network’s theme music is a certified slapper.
Cowher is on its main pregame show, “The NFL Today,” which also adds one-time Steelers quarterback Russell Wilson and fellow recent retiree Kyle Long to its studio crew. CBS announcers include Jim Nantz and Ian Eagle, while the color commentary rotation stars the oldest Watt brother .
What you’ll need to watch: A pay TV package, or an indoor TV antenna for free over-the-air viewing. Local CBS games also stream on Paramount+.
Main window: Sunday afternoon (in-market fans)
Playoffs: 1 wild-card game, 1 divisional game, NFC Championship Game
Like CBS, Fox splits Sunday afternoons between early 1 p.m. action and later 4:05/4:25 p.m. matchups. Its centerpiece is branded as “America’s Game of the Week.” Unlike CBS, Fox has a dancing robot named Cleatus . It’s the nominal network for the NFC as well.
Kevin Burkhardt, Joe Davis and Adam Amin are the lead play-by-play voices. Burkhardt pairs with Tom Brady, while Davis calls games alongside Greg Olsen. Amin is partnered with newcomer Drew Brees, who is fresh off his Pro Football Hall of Fame induction. Some Spanish-language broadcasts are available on Fox Deportes.
What you’ll need to watch: A pay TV package, or an antenna for free over-the-air viewing. Local Fox games also stream on Fox One.
Main window: Sunday afternoon (out-of-market fans)
These two are the access points for all non-national matchups that aren’t on regional CBS or Fox.
NFL Sunday Ticket has full games. It’s exclusive to YouTube and YouTube TV. Those without a YouTube TV plan can still get NFL Sunday Ticket as a primetime channel through the standard YouTube app.
RedZone is the whip-around program that jumps around the slate to cover scoring drives. This is the place for Scott Hanson , “the witching hour” and chaotic octobox split screens. It can be added to NFL Sunday Ticket, and it’s included on some high-end pay TV sports plans.
RedZone also lives on NFL+ Premium, which can be bundled with the ESPN Unlimited plan.
What you’ll need to watch: An NFL Sunday Ticket subscription through YouTube TV or the YouTube app; NFL RedZone access through select pay TV packages, ESPN Unlimited or NFL+ Premium.
Playoffs: 2 wild-card games, 1 divisional game
This is the faithful home of “Sunday Night Football” each weekend. And because everything has to be confusing, the NBC lineup opens with a Wednesday night season premiere. At least SNF has a consistent 8:20 p.m. start time.
Mike Tirico and Cris Collinsworth are in the booth, with Melissa Stark reporting from the sidelines. Carrie Underwood sings about waiting all day for Sunday night . NBC’s “Football Night in America” pregame show brings on Tomlin in his first gig since leaving the Steelers. Telemundo has the telecasts in Spanish.
The network has two extra Saturday offerings for Week 17. One is exclusive to Peacock, and both matchups will be announced later in the season. The same goes for NBC’s Week 18 regular-season finale.
“Sunday Night Football” is subject to flex scheduling — games can be swapped in and out of the window twice between Weeks 5-10 and any time from Weeks 11-17. This allows executives to pick games with greater playoff implications, though it leaves the actual ticket holders in a bind.
What you’ll need to watch: A pay TV package, or an antenna for free over-the-air viewing, or a Peacock account with the live sports plan.
Playoffs: 1 wild-card game, 1 divisional game, Super Bowl LXI
The Disney networks combine to cover 17 “Monday Night Football” games. Ten of those are on both ABC and ESPN, with another seven exclusive to the latter. The oft-maligned “Monday Night Football” doubleheader is now a thing of the past.
MNF kickoffs have 8:15 p.m. starts, and their schedule flexes can happen any time in Weeks 12-17. The two Saturday ABC/ESPN matchups in Week 18 will be set as the postseason picture sharpens.
ESPN is preparing for its first Super Bowl broadcast ever on Feb. 14, 2027. It will be simulcast on ABC.
Joe Buck handles play-by-play for MNF. He’s joined by analyst Troy Aikman, plus the sideline duo of Lisa Salters and Laura Rutledge. Spanish-language airings can be found on ESPN Deportes. For 12 regular-season games and the Super Bowl, ESPN2 offers an alternate “ManningCast,” in which Eli and Peyton Manning watch the games with famous fans. Guests have ranged from Bill Belichick to Lil Wayne .
What you’ll need to watch: A pay TV package, or an antenna for ABC, or an ESPN Unlimited account.
Main window: Thursday night
Playoffs: 1 wild-card game
Most weeks begin with “Thursday Night Football,” which kicks off at 8:15 p.m. Those games are behind the Prime paywall, but they’re free over the air in the participants’ home markets. Flex rules around TNF are a bit less hectic, with two allotments between Weeks 13-17.
Despite it not being on a Thursday, this is also where you can find the Steelers’ Black Friday showdown with the Broncos. It starts at 3 p.m. and not in the usual primetime window.
TNF is called by Al Michaels and Kirk Herbstreit, with Kaylee Hartung on sideline duty. Herbstreit loves dogs ; Michaels hates vegetables . Prime has Spanish-language coverage and advanced stat broadcast options within its app. Among the pregame and postgame personalities are former All-Pros Tony Gonzalez, Richard Sherman and Andrew Whitworth.
What you’ll need to watch: Amazon Prime. TNF is also free on Twitch with a registered account.
The league-owned media outlet is now under ESPN’s purview, thanks to a blockbuster deal that gave the NFL a 10 percent ownership stake in “The Worldwide Leader in Sports.” As of July 30, NFL Network is integrated into the ESPN Unlimited plan. It can also…

full_text:
Running back Travis Homer could be a game-day call-up in certain weeks. Justin K. Aller / Getty Images
The Steelers continued to build out their roster Monday with 14 practice-squad additions. The most noteworthy takeaway remains the player who isn’t yet signed: Elandon Roberts.
The physical inside linebacker was one of the surprise omissions from the 53-man roster . As of Monday evening, the 32-year-old had yet to sign with any team.
“I’m not closing the door on that by any means,” Steelers GM Omar Khan said Monday afternoon. “I have a lot of respect for E Rob. We have some history with him, and he’s done a good job. I love the the player and love the person. Certainly not closing the door.”
If the Steelers do intend to bring Roberts back, there aren’t many roster spots left, as the team has just three places remaining. Those final players should be announced in the coming days. Let’s take a deep look at the known practice players, ranked by their chances of contributing this season.
Safety depth was already a concern throughout camp — that was before the Steelers placed DeShon Elliott on injured reserve, forcing him to miss at least the first four games. Cut by the Colts at the end of camp, Thomas now sits fourth on the Steelers’ depth chart behind Jaquan Brisker, Rayshawn Jenkins and rookie Robert Spears-Jennings. Thomas began his career as a 2022 UDFA in Dallas, where he overlapped with Mike McCarthy. Before that, the 6-foot, 212-pound safety was a core special teamer at Georgia Tech. That’s likely the area he’d contribute most, even if there are injuries to the safeties. Thomas has appeared in 36 games between 2023 and 2025, with four starts. He’s recorded 62 tackles and five passes defended.
A special-teams ace who often served as the personal protector on the punt unit during training camp, Homer was firmly in the RB3 competition. (In fact, I expected him to make the team on my final projection .) However, the Steelers chose Eli Heidrenreich’s return ability and offensive skill set over a four-phase special teamer like Homer. The Steelers might consider elevating Homer for particular matchups, or in the event any of the core special teamers are injured.
A 27-year-old journeyman, Otomewo enjoyed his most productive year as a pro last season. The 6-5, 282-pound defensive lineman appeared in 12 games, with nine tackles and one sack. Through most of camp, he sat right on the bubble. The Steelers opted for youth over experience.
Nichols had a legitimate case to make the 53-man roster over Heidenreich. While Heidenreich returns kicks and is a hybrid player who brings a different element to the RB room, Nichols is the more polished pure running back. His vision and quick first step was evident throughout the preseason, as he carried the ball 20 times for 87 yards and a touchdown. If the Steelers suffer an injury to Jaylen Warren or Rico Dowdle during the season, Nichols is the player I’d promote to the active roster to split carries with the other healthy lead back.
The Steelers showed how they feel about Hurleman by making him a team captain for the third preseason game. During the three preseason games, he recorded seven catches for 99 yards. If the Steelers lose a return man or a receiver, Hurleman would be in consideration for a game-day promotion.
When the Steelers opened camp, Smith surprisingly trotted out with the first-team offense. He played well in Latrobe, most notably in the Saturday Night Lights practice. However, he was always a long shot to make the team. A camp injury didn’t help, either. At 6-2 and 220, Smith has brings size and some familiarity with Aaron Rodgers from their time together with the Jets. If the Steelers lost an outside receiver to injury, he might get the call over Hurleman. The main reason I put Hurleman ahead on this list is because of his return ability.
A former five-year starter at West Virginia, Nester has spent the early part of his career on the Steelers’ practice squad. He showed some versatility in the preseason, playing guard and tackle. By dealing Broderick Jones, the Steelers took some depth away from that position group. Nester also has position flex, with is critical for a backup.
The Steelers typically carry five inside linebackers on the 53-man roster, but this is one of the positions that felt the numbers crunch of a four-QB roster. At 6-2 and 250 pounds, Windmon has the body type to be a physical, downhill inside linebacker. He registered six tackles (one for loss) over 50 defensive snaps this preseason. He also has the body type to contribute on special teams. Given how thin the Steelers are at inside linebacker, Windmon is near the top of this list.
If the Steelers lost a safety, they’d have to determine how they want to reshuffle the pieces. If it’s anything like last year, they could be one injury away from playing Jalen Ramsey at safety full-time. If that’s the case, they would need some depth at nickel corner and Slaughter could help provide it.
Castro joined the Steelers as a UDFA a year ago. He impressed enough during the joint practice that the Tampa Bay Buccaneers scooped him up for part of the 2025 season. A hybrid DB at Iowa who played the nickel, Castro is a smaller body type at 5-11 and 203. Given the lack of depth at safety, he’ll be an option in the event of injury.
Baugh spent he 2025 season on the Steelers practice squad and will likely spend most of his 2026 season in the same way. At 6-3 and nearly 300 pounds, he’s a thick and physical player with low center of gravity. He’s an option as a depth nose tackle, mostly.
At one point in camp, Jones was running with the second-team offensive line before an injury. Brock Hoffman is likely the first guard off the bench. Gennings Dunker is next. Then, the Steelers would have to decide between Jones and Nester.
The German-born Welschof is a free roster spot as part of the NFL’s international player pathway. He was making solid progress before a knee injury a few years back. Given the quality of the depth ahead of him, it may take a lot for him to get an opportunity on the active roster.
Tight end appeared to be a position where the Steelers might trim in order to keep four QBs. However, they ultimately decided to keep Robert Tonyan on the 53-man roster. Given the depth at this position and the fact that McRee dropped a couple passes in preseason games, he’s last on this list.

title: Adam Peters and Dan Quinn are confident in the Commanders. Now, they have to be right Washington's general manager and coach are pitching that their team is prepared for the real games to start. We'll see soon. Barry Svrluga 15
